explanation: The plants were meant to grow cheap food for enslaved workers on British plantations in the Caribbean. Bligh delivered them on a later voyage, and breadfruit became a Jamaican staple.

claims.text: HMS Bounty, under William Bligh, was carrying breadfruit plants from Tahiti, bound for the Caribbean, when its crew mutinied.
The Bounty's cargo of young plants was breadfruit, not sugar cane, coconut or banana.
The breadfruit was meant to provide cheap food for enslaved workers on British plantations in the Caribbean.
Bligh delivered breadfruit plants to the Caribbean on a later voyage, and breadfruit became a staple food in Jamaica.

evidence.restatement: HMS Bounty under Bligh was carrying breadfruit plants from Tahiti for the West Indies when the crew mutinied in 1789.
The cargo was breadfruit, not sugar cane, coconut or banana.
The breadfruit was meant as cheap food for enslaved workers on British Caribbean plantations.
Bligh delivered breadfruit on a second voyage (HMS Providence, 1793), and it became a staple in Jamaica.
HMS Bounty under William Bligh left Tahiti in April 1789 with breadfruit plants for the West Indies, and the crew mutinied on 28 April 1789.
The voyage's purpose was breadfruit, not sugar cane, coconut or banana.
The aim was cheap food for enslaved people on British Caribbean plantations.
